subject: Economics
description: GATT to WTO transition, MFN, NT, agreements, ministerial conferences, India's positions

questions.stem: The World Trade Organization (WTO) was established in:

options.option_text: 1995 (succeeding GATT, after the Marrakesh Agreement of April 1994)

questions.explanation: WTO — established 1 January 1995, headquartered at Geneva, Switzerland. Successor to the GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, 1947 — only a treaty, not an organisation). Created by the URUGUAY ROUND of GATT negotiations (1986-94), formalised by the MARRAKESH AGREEMENT (April 1994). India is a founding member. As of 2024 — 166 member countries (Comoros and Timor-Leste joined Aug 2024). Director-General — Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala (Nigeria; first woman, first African to hold the post; reappointed for second 4-year term ending 2029).

questions.stem: The 'Most Favoured Nation' (MFN) principle of the WTO requires that:

options.option_text: Members trade only with their favoured allies
Any trade concession given to one WTO member must be extended to ALL other members on equal terms (no discrimination among trading partners)
Most countries get preferential rates
MFN status is awarded only to developed countries

questions.explanation: MFN — Article I of GATT, the cornerstone non-discrimination principle. If country A gives B a 5% tariff on a product, A must extend the same 5% to ALL other WTO members. Exceptions: (1) Free Trade Agreements / Customs Unions (NAFTA, EU, ASEAN) — preferential treatment within bloc allowed; (2) Generalised System of Preferences (GSP) — developed countries can give better access to developing countries; (3) National-security exceptions. NATIONAL TREATMENT (Art III) — once goods are imported, they must be treated the same as domestic goods (no discriminatory taxes/regulations). India revoked Pakistan's MFN status after Pulwama attack (Feb 2019); Pakistan never granted India MFN status post 1996.

questions.stem: The TRIPS Agreement under the WTO deals with:

options.option_text: Tariffs on industrial products
Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights (patents, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets)
Travel and tourism
Trade in agriculture only

questions.explanation: TRIPS (Trade-Related Aspects of Intellectual Property Rights) — adopted 1995 alongside WTO. Sets MINIMUM IP standards: patents 20 years; copyright life of author + 50 years (often extended); trademarks renewable. India had to amend its 1970 Patents Act in 2005 to introduce product patents on pharmaceuticals (had been process patents only — that's how Indian generics industry like Cipla, Dr Reddy's grew). DOHA DECLARATION 2001 — TRIPS + Public Health: countries can issue compulsory licences for affordable access to essential medicines (HIV, TB, etc.). Section 3(d) of Indian Patents Act — prevents 'evergreening' (Novartis Glivec case 2013, SC ruled against Novartis). Other key WTO agreements: GATS (services), AoA (agriculture), SPS (sanitary measures), TBT (technical barriers).

questions.stem: The DOHA round of WTO negotiations (started 2001) is also called the:

options.option_text: Tokyo round
Doha Development Agenda
Bretton Woods round
Geneva accord

questions.explanation: Doha Round (2001-) — formally the DOHA DEVELOPMENT AGENDA (DDA), launched at the 4th Ministerial Conference in Doha, Qatar. Focus: development concerns of poor countries, especially in agriculture, services, IPR. Major sticking points: (1) Agricultural subsidies — developed countries (US, EU) heavily subsidise farms (~$300 bn/year); developing countries demand cuts. India + China — peace clause for public food stockholding (e.g., MSP-based PDS). (2) Special + Differential Treatment for developing countries. (3) NAMA — non-agricultural market access. After 20+ years, Doha Round is largely STALLED — not formally concluded; the multilateral path has yielded to bilateral / plurilateral FTAs (TPP, RCEP, etc.). India has historically resisted reduction in its food subsidies, leveraging the food security argument.

questions.stem: The WTO's HIGHEST decision-making body is the:

options.option_text: Director-General's office
Ministerial Conference (meets every two years)
General Council
Secretariat

questions.explanation: WTO structure (top-down): (1) MINISTERIAL CONFERENCE — supreme body; meets every 2 years; trade ministers of ALL members. Recent ones: MC11 Buenos Aires 2017; MC12 Geneva 2022 (reached deal on fisheries subsidies, COVID vaccine waiver); MC13 Abu Dhabi Feb-Mar 2024. MC14 scheduled for 2026 in Cameroon. (2) GENERAL COUNCIL — meets between Ministerial Conferences (about 8-12 times/year); also doubles as the Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) and the Trade Policy Review Body (TPRB). (3) Sub-councils — Goods, Services, IPRs. (4) Secretariat (Geneva) — ~625 staff; led by the Director-General. Decisions traditionally by CONSENSUS (no formal vote); each country has equal voice (1 country, 1 vote in case of vote — unlike IMF's weighted voting).

questions.stem: The WTO's Dispute Settlement Body (DSB) — important in resolving trade conflicts — has been hampered since 2019 because:

options.option_text: Members lost interest in disputes
The US has blocked appointment of new judges to the Appellate Body, leaving it without quorum to hear appeals
WTO ran out of funds
Disputes were transferred to the UN

questions.explanation: WTO Dispute Settlement Body — long considered the 'crown jewel' of the WTO (binding dispute resolution, unlike most international bodies). Process: panel report → appellate body review → adoption → compliance. APPELLATE BODY — needs minimum 3 of 7 judges to hear an appeal. Since 2017, the US (under Trump and continued under Biden) has BLOCKED new Appellate Body appointments — citing concerns over judicial overreach. By Dec 2019, the Appellate Body fell below quorum and has been NON-FUNCTIONAL since. Workarounds: MPIA (Multi-Party Interim Appeal Arbitration Arrangement, 2020) — 26 countries (incl. EU, China, but not US, India) agreed to use Article 25 arbitration as appeal substitute. India has been wary, fearing similar 'overreach' on agricultural subsidy issues.

questions.stem: Which agreement of the WTO seeks to reduce trade-distorting agricultural subsidies and is a contentious area for India?

options.option_text: GATS
AoA — Agreement on Agriculture (with Green / Amber / Blue boxes for different subsidy types)
TRIPS
TBT

questions.explanation: AoA — entered force 1995. Classifies subsidies into BOXES: GREEN BOX (non/minimally trade-distorting — research, environmental, infrastructure; allowed without limit); AMBER BOX (trade-distorting — direct price support, input subsidies; capped at 10% of value of agricultural production for developing countries — the 'de minimis' level); BLUE BOX (production-limiting, with restrictions). India's MSP + PDS system risks crossing the de minimis threshold. BALI MINISTERIAL 2013 — peace clause for India: developing countries can exceed AMBER limits for public stockholding for food security WITHOUT being challenged at WTO, until a permanent solution. The 'PERMANENT SOLUTION' on PSH remains India's key demand at MC13 (2024) and beyond. SCM — Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures (industrial subsidies).

questions.stem: The WTO's Trade Facilitation Agreement (TFA), which entered into force in February 2017, is primarily aimed at which of the following objectives?

options.option_text: Eliminating all tariffs on agricultural exports of LDCs by 2020
Simplifying customs procedures and reducing red tape at national borders
Harmonising intellectual property laws across all WTO member countries
Regulating cross-border investment flows among developing economies

questions.explanation: B is correct: the TFA — WTO's first multilateral deal since 1994 — focuses on expediting movement, release and clearance of goods and reducing customs red tape. It does not deal with tariffs on LDC exports (that is partly the Nairobi Package), nor IP (TRIPS) nor investment flows (TRIMs).

questions.stem: A foreign bank opens a branch in India to offer retail banking services to Indian customers. Under the WTO's General Agreement on Trade in Services (GATS), this constitutes which mode of supply?

options.option_text: Mode 1 — service supplied from the foreign country to India remotely
Mode 2 — Indian consumer travels abroad to receive the banking service
Mode 3 — commercial presence established by the supplier in India
Mode 4 — temporary movement of bank personnel across national borders

questions.explanation: C is correct: Mode 3 (Commercial Presence) covers a foreign service supplier establishing a branch, subsidiary or joint venture in the consumer's territory. Mode 1 would be internet-based cross-border services; Mode 2 is like medical tourism; Mode 4 involves individual employees moving temporarily, not the entity itself.

questions.stem: The WTO Agreement on Trade-Related Investment Measures (TRIMs) explicitly prohibits investment measures that are inconsistent with GATT's national-treatment and quantitative-restriction disciplines. Which of the following domestic measures does TRIMs directly prohibit?

options.option_text: Local content requirements mandating use of domestically produced inputs
Differential corporate tax rates applicable to foreign-owned enterprises
Restrictions on repatriation of profits earned by foreign companies
Reservation of strategic sectors exclusively for state-owned entities

questions.explanation: A is correct: the Illustrative List annexed to TRIMs explicitly names local content requirements (requiring investors to buy or use domestic goods) as inconsistent with GATT Article III national treatment. Profit repatriation restrictions, differential corporate taxes, and sector reservations for SOEs are not covered by TRIMs — they may fall under BITs or GATS instead.

questions.stem: WTO's Agreement on Agriculture classifies domestic support into 'boxes'. Which of the following measures qualifies as a 'Green Box' subsidy and is therefore exempt from reduction commitments?

options.option_text: Minimum Support Price payments linked to current crop production levels
Direct income support to farmers fully decoupled from current production
Input subsidies on fertilisers tied to the quantity of crops produced
Deficiency payments made when market prices fall below a support price

questions.explanation: B is correct: Green Box subsidies must be government-funded, not involve price support, and cause minimal trade distortion. Decoupled income support — where payment amounts are fixed and do not depend on what or how much is produced — is the classic Green Box instrument. MSP-linked payments, deficiency payments, and output-linked fertiliser subsidies are all trade-distorting and fall under the Amber Box.

questions.stem: India's public food-stockholding program, which procures grain at Minimum Support Prices for distribution under the National Food Security Act, has repeatedly triggered WTO disputes because it is alleged to breach which specific ceiling?

options.option_text: The Blue Box cap on production-limiting subsidy payments for developing members
The 10% de minimis Aggregate Measure of Support threshold for developing countries
The Green Box ceiling for decoupled income support set by the WTO Secretariat
The Special Safeguard Mechanism threshold activated by import price surges

questions.explanation: B is correct: Developing countries get a 10% de minimis AMS exemption (developed countries get 5%). India's procurement at MSP — compared against the 1986–88 external reference price — is alleged to breach this 10% ceiling for rice and wheat. The 2013 Bali 'peace clause', extended at Nairobi 2015, temporarily shields such stockholding from WTO challenge. Green Box, Blue Box, and SSM are unrelated to this specific dispute.

questions.stem: In the WTO's Agreement on Agriculture, the 'external reference price' used to compute a country's Aggregate Measure of Support (AMS) for a commodity is fixed at average world prices during which base period — a choice that significantly inflates apparent support levels for developing-country MSP programs today?

options.option_text: 1980–1985, reflecting pre-Uruguay Round international commodity prices
1986–1988, the base period locked in during the Uruguay Round negotiations
1990–1994, the final years before the WTO came into existence in 1995
1995–2000, the first five years after WTO's Agreement on Agriculture took effect

questions.explanation: B is correct: the 1986–1988 external reference price (ERP) is the benchmark frozen into the Agreement on Agriculture. Since global food prices were low in that period, comparing today's MSP (in nominal rupee terms converted to USD) against the 1986–88 ERP makes India's support appear disproportionately large — the crux of the India-US/EU subsidy dispute. The other periods are plausible distractors but none was used as the AoA base.

questions.stem: The WTO's Agreement on Government Procurement (GPA) is described as a 'plurilateral' rather than a 'multilateral' agreement. What is the precise legal consequence of this classification for WTO members who have not acceded to it, such as India?

options.option_text: All WTO members must implement GPA within five years of their accession to WTO
GPA obligations bind only WTO members that have explicitly signed and acceded to it
GPA is enforced by the WTO DSB but applies exclusively to developed-country members
GPA applies to developing members only after they cross a WTO-set GDP per capita threshold

questions.explanation: B is correct: plurilateral agreements (unlike multilateral ones such as GATT, GATS, TRIPS) create rights and obligations only for the WTO members who choose to accede to them. India holds observer status in GPA but has not joined, so its government procurement remains outside GPA disciplines. This contrasts with multilateral WTO agreements that automatically bind all members upon accession. Developed-country-only and GDP-threshold-based limitations do not exist under GPA's actual terms.
